questions.question: A pickup truck with 20 times the mass of a cyclist and his bike creeps across a car park at half a metre per second, while the cyclist speeds along a flat road at 10 metres per second. Brakes giving the same steady force are put on both at the same moment. Which one takes more time to stop?
questions.answer: Neither, since the two carry equal momentum
choices: Neither, since the two carry equal momentum
The truck, since its mass is far greater
The cyclist, since his speed is far greater
The cyclist, since his energy is far greater
questions.context: Momentum is mass times velocity, so 20 times the mass at a twentieth of the speed is exactly the cyclist's momentum, and a steady force takes momentum away at a steady rate: the two stop together. The cyclist does carry 20 times the energy of motion, so he rolls 20 times as far while braking, but for no longer. At the same speed as the bike, the truck would carry 20 times the momentum and need 20 times as long to stop.
questions.grade_note: High-school physical science (NGSS HS-PS2, TEKS IPC 5) defines momentum as mass times velocity, and the heavy-slow against light-fast comparison is the standard way it is taught apart from mass, speed and kinetic energy.

questions.question: A cue ball strikes a still ball of the same mass squarely and stops dead, and the struck ball rolls on across the cloth of the pool table. It slows, and a few seconds later both balls lie still. Their total momentum, large just after the hit, is now zero. Does that break the law of conservation of momentum?
questions.answer: No, since the cloth's friction is an outside force
choices: No, since the cloth's friction is an outside force
No, since the momentum has all turned into heat
No, since a still ball keeps its momentum stored
Yes, since total momentum can never change at all
questions.context: Total momentum stays the same only while no outside force acts. In the split-second hit, friction is far too small to matter, so the struck ball leaves with all the momentum the cue ball brought; afterwards the cloth's friction pushes back on it and passes that momentum to the table and Earth, far too massive to be seen to move. It is the ball's energy of motion, not its momentum, that ends up as heat.
questions.grade_note: NGSS HS-PS2-2 teaches that total momentum is conserved when there is no net outside force, and a 9th-grader is expected to say when that condition holds.

questions.question: A hunter fires the same rifle twice. The first time he holds the butt loosely, a little way off his shoulder, and the rifle slams back into him. The second time he pulls it tight against his shoulder, and the kick is far gentler. Why does the tight hold soften the kick?
questions.answer: His body and the rifle move back as one mass
choices: His body and the rifle move back as one mass
His grip cancels out the momentum of the kick
His grip makes the kick last a shorter time
The bullet leaves with less momentum than before
questions.context: Before the shot the total momentum is zero, so whatever moves back must carry as much momentum as the bullet and its gases carry forward. Held tight, the rifle and the hunter's body take that momentum together, and so much mass moves back only slowly; held loosely, the light rifle alone picks up speed and then strikes his shoulder hard. The bullet's momentum is the same both times.
questions.grade_note: Recoil is the standard high-school example of momentum conserved from rest (NGSS HS-PS2-2), and asking which masses move together is the 9th-grade step beyond the bare rule.

questions.question: Two pair skaters stand still, face to face, on smooth ice, and he has twice her mass. They press their palms together and push off each other, and the two glide apart in opposite directions across the rink. Which of them glides away faster?
questions.answer: She does, with as much momentum as he has
choices: She does, with as much momentum as he has
She does, with more momentum than he has
He does, since he gives the harder push
Neither, since they glide off equally fast
questions.context: They start still, so their total momentum is zero, and after the push their momenta must be equal in size and opposite in direction. Momentum is mass times velocity, so she, with half his mass, glides off at twice his speed. Each pushes on the other just as hard for the same moment, which is why the two momenta match.
questions.grade_note: Two skaters pushing apart is the textbook 'explosion' case of momentum conservation in high-school physical science (NGSS HS-PS2-2).

questions.question: René Descartes taught in his Principles of Philosophy (1644) that the total 'quantity of motion', each body's size times its speed, never changes. Two equal lumps of soft clay fly at each other at the same speed, meet head on, stick and stop dead. Counted Descartes's way, their motion is lost. Christiaan Huygens found a count that is kept in every collision. What did his count take into account?
questions.answer: The direction each body moves in
choices: The direction each body moves in
The square of each body's speed
The heat each collision gives off
The push each body gives the other
questions.context: Counting motion one way as plus and the other way as minus, the lumps held plus one and minus one before they met, a total of nothing, and nothing after: the quantity was kept. Huygens also found that mass times the square of the speed adds up the same in collisions of hard, bouncing bodies, but not of soft ones like clay, which turn their motion into heat. His directed count, mass times velocity, is now called momentum.
questions.grade_note: High-school physics teaches that momentum is a vector, so opposite motions cancel, and Huygens's correction of Descartes is the history of how that was found.

questions.question: Christopher Wren and Christiaan Huygens gave the Royal Society rules for collisions of hard bodies in 1668 and 1669, and John Wallis rules for soft ones. Isaac Newton tested such rules with balls of steel, glass, cork and wound wool on ten-foot threads. Steel balls sprang apart almost as fast as they met, wool ones at little over half that speed. What did he find about each pair's total momentum?
questions.answer: It stayed the same for every kind of ball
choices: It stayed the same for every kind of ball
It stayed the same only for the steel balls
It stayed the same only for equal-sized balls
It shrank in the pairs that sprang apart slowly
questions.context: Newton read each ball's speed from the arc it swung through, and for equal and unequal balls alike the motion one ball gained in one direction matched the motion the other gained in the opposite one, within 3 inches on his ten-foot threads. The rule held 'as well in soft as in hard bodies'; only the bounce differed. A soft collision loses energy of motion to heat and squashing, never momentum.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science separates elastic from inelastic collisions and teaches that momentum is conserved in both; Newton's pendulum test is the experiment behind that claim.

questions.question: John Paul Stapp, an Air Force doctor, rode the rocket sled Sonic Wind No. 1 in New Mexico in December 1954 to learn what a human body can survive. Its rockets took him from a standstill to 632 miles per hour in five seconds, and then the sled was brought to a stop in 1.4 seconds. Which part of the run pressed hardest on his body?
questions.answer: The stop, which changed his speed in the least time
choices: The stop, which changed his speed in the least time
The start, when the rockets drove him forward hard
The top speed, when he was moving at his fastest
Start and stop alike, as both changed his speed equally
questions.context: His speed rose by 632 miles per hour and fell by the same amount, so he gained and lost the same momentum, but the stop took a little over a quarter of the time, so its force was far greater, reaching 46.2 g. Moving fast at a steady speed presses on no one; only a change of speed does. Textbooks of the day put 18 g as the limit of human tolerance, and Stapp, strapped into a strong harness, lived through more than twice that.
questions.grade_note: NGSS HS-PS2-3 asks students to reason about the force on a body in a collision from the time it lasts, and Stapp's sled runs are the classic test of what a stop can do to a person.

questions.question: Béla Barényi, an engineer at Daimler-Benz, doubted the long-held view that a safe car had to be rigid. His patent, granted in 1952, gave a car a stiff cabin between a front and back built to crumple in a crash, and a 1959 Mercedes was the first car built to it. How does a front that crumples protect the people inside?
questions.answer: It makes the stop take longer, so the push on them is gentler
choices: It makes the stop take longer, so the push on them is gentler
It makes the stop take less time, so the crash is over sooner
It soaks up the car's momentum, so none of it reaches them
It springs back, so the car rebounds off whatever it hits
questions.context: A car hitting a wall must lose all its momentum whatever it is made of; folding metal stretches that loss over more time, so the average force on the people in the cabin is smaller. A rigid car stops abruptly, which makes the jolt far harsher. The crumpled metal stays crumpled, taking in energy of motion, while the stiff cabin keeps its space around the people.
questions.grade_note: NGSS HS-PS2-3 has students design a device that lowers the force in a collision by lengthening it, and Barényi's crumple zone is the standard real case.

questions.question: A girl jumps down from a low wall onto hard ground twice, from the same height each time. On the first jump she lands stiff-legged. On the second she bends her knees as her feet touch the ground and lets her body sink down. What is the same in both landings?
choices: The change in her momentum
The force from the ground on her legs
The time it takes her to stop
How sharply she slows to a stop
questions.context: She meets the ground at the same speed both times and ends at rest, so the ground must take away the same momentum. Bending her knees stretches that over a longer time, so she slows less sharply and the force on her legs is smaller. A car's air bag, the crushing foam of a helmet and a catcher's padded glove work the same way.
questions.grade_note: Impulse, the change in momentum that a force gives over a time, is taught in 9th-grade physical science with landing and catching as its everyday cases (NGSS HS-PS2-3).
